blocks.text: Email injection occurs when user input is placed into a mail message or protocol command without stripping CR/LF or MIME structure. Typical sinks are contact and invite forms, password-reset mailers, "send to a friend" features and webmail clients (IMAP/SMTP command injection). Impact includes spamming, phishing from a trusted sender, reset-link redirection, header spoofing and data exfiltration via added recipients.

items: To, From, Subject, Reply-To and custom headers built from form input
Additional `Cc:` and `Bcc:` recipients added with CR/LF
Body injection through a header that ends the header block early
MIME boundary and content-type manipulation, HTML injection in HTML email
IMAP/SMTP command injection in webmail and mail-proxy features
Email-address parsing differences (quoted local parts, comments, encoded words) that bypass validation or domain allow-lists
Password-reset and invitation mailers where the recipient can be duplicated

blocks.text: Use mailboxes you own. Add a second recipient you control through a CRLF in the field and check which mailbox receives the message and with what headers. Compare how the validator and the mail library parse the same address; mismatches create allow-list bypasses. For webmail and mail proxies, inject protocol commands such as `NOOP` and observe protocol-level errors. Do not email third parties or send bulk messages.
See `email-injection-payloads.txt`. Replace the addresses with mailboxes you control.

sections.label: CRLF header injection in an email field (add recipients)
Body injection (end header block, start body)
Address-parsing confusion (validator vs mail library disagree on the domain)
Local-part trick with the target domain as a sub-label of a controlled domain
Reset / invitation duplication (array or duplicated parameter: see HTTP-Parameter-Pollution)
HTML injection in HTML email (link or image to a controlled host)
SMTP command injection (webmail or mail proxy sending to a back end; in a field that becomes an SMTP command argument)
IMAP command injection (a mailbox name or message number placed into a command; marker commands only)
Mail header spoofing checks (SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment; send only to your own mailbox)
Open mail relay checks (run only against hosts you own)
